info.summary: Pay-per-call video generation and speech over x402. The unpaid 402 is the quote.
info.description: Frontier text-to-video models and TTS, priced per call in USDC on Base or Solana. No account and no API key: an unpaid POST answers 402 with the exact price for the body you sent, and paying that 402 is the whole authentication story. Quote and charge come from one function, so the number advertised is the number that settles.
info.x-guidance:
kino402 sells frontier text-to-video and text-to-speech per call, in USDC on Base or Solana over x402. No account, no API key, no minimum.

THE QUOTE IS THE 402. POST an unpaid request to /v1/generate or /v1/audio/tts and the 402 that comes back carries the exact price for the body you sent — not a rate card, the number for that call. Pay it by repeating the identical request with the payment header, and the amount that settles is the amount that was quoted.

Headers: send X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, or PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2. The v1 envelope is the 402 response body; the v2 envelope is standard base64 in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED response header. Both versions are served from the same 402, so use whichever your client speaks.

Rails: Base — USDC 0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913, network "base" in x402 v1 and "eip155:8453" in v2; Solana — USDC EPjFWdd5AufqSSqeM2qN1xzybapC8G4wEGGkZwyTDt1v, network "solana" in x402 v1 and "solana:5eykt4UsFv8P8NJdTREpY1vzqKqZKvdp" in v2. Every rail carries the SAME quote for a given request — a second rail is a second way to pay, never a second price. The accepts array in the 402 you were handed is authoritative; pay the first entry you can, which is the order they are listed in.

POST is how you buy. A GET or HEAD on a paid route answers a reference 402 so a prober can read the terms without spending, but a payment presented on GET is refused without settling.

/v1/generate is asynchronous. A paid POST returns {job_id, status_url} once the render is accepted upstream. Poll GET /v1/jobs/{id} — free and unauthenticated — until status is "completed" (the mp4 is at video_url) or "failed". A clip usually takes 1-6 minutes. The video_url expires: download it promptly.

An image is an OPENING FRAME, not a style reference: on a model with an image-to-video path (see image_to_video in GET /v1/models) the clip starts on exactly that picture. Anywhere else an image is a 400, never silently dropped. On a paid request the Worker fetches the URL once before anything is claimed, and a URL that does not answer 200 with a JPEG, PNG or WebP is a 400 with nothing charged — an unpaid quote never fetches it.

/v1/audio/tts is synchronous. A paid POST returns the mp3 in the response body.

A /v1/forms/ route sells a FORMAT rather than a model: you send a structured brief — for the UGC form, a product name and one to five selling points; for the hero loop, one product photo; for the launch teaser, the line being announced; for the faceless explainer, a topic and its beats — and the service compiles it into the prompt and renders it on your behalf. It is priced as the renderer plus a compile fee, quoted in the same 402, delivered as the same job id, and the compiled prompt comes back with it so you can inspect or reuse the shot. GET /v1/models publishes every field of every form with its bounds and its default.

A /v1/prompts/ route sells that compiler on its own, flat-priced and synchronous: the same brief in, and {prompt, render_plan, compiler} straight back in the response body — no job, no polling, no video. It is the cheapest thing in the catalog and it is the honest way to evaluate the format before buying a render, or to buy the prompt craft alone if you already have renderer credits. The prompt it returns is a valid `prompt` for POST /v1/generate, and render_plan carries the model, seconds, resolution and aspect ratio it was written for.

GET /v1/models carries the full rate card: every model id, its parameter ranges, the rate formula it is priced from, and a worked example price. Read it before you pick a model — the cheapest and the most expensive video call in the catalog differ by more than two orders of magnitude.

billable_unit.note: One call. A single signed authorization buys exactly one call at the amount that call's own 402 quoted, and the whole quoted amount settles or nothing does — there is no partial, metered or per-second billing and no charge is ever split across a retry. kino402 prices are parametric, so the band published here is the floor and the ceiling this resource can quote; the unpaid 402 answering the body you actually sent is the authority on the number, and it is the number that settles.

hold.note: None. Verification is a read at the facilitator (verifyPayment in worker/kino.js), so nothing is reserved, escrowed or held: the signed authorization moves no funds until it is submitted at settle, which runs in ctx.waitUntil after the response has already been sent. An authorization that never reaches settle is simply never submitted, and no balance of yours was ever encumbered while it was outstanding.

idempotency.key: sha256(signed authorization: network + payer + nonce on EVM, network + transaction on Solana)
idempotency.note: There is no idempotency-key header. The key is the signed authorization itself, read out of the payment header — PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2, X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, and PAYMENT-SIGNATURE is the one read when a request carries both: on Base the SHA-256 of the network, the payer address and the EIP-3009 nonce, on Solana of the network and the serialized transaction's decoded bytes (claimKeyOf in worker/kino.js). Re-encoding the same authorization — whitespace, key order, the other protocol version, a respelled base64 transaction — is therefore the same key, and a payment missing its network's authorization field is refused 402 `malformed_payment_header` before anything is claimed. The key is claimed single-use by claimPaymentOnce after the payment verifies and before any work is ordered. A second request carrying the same authorization, concurrently or an hour later, is answered 402 with invalidReason `payment_already_used` and the live terms re-offered: it submits no render, compiles no prompt, synthesises no audio and settles nothing. Sign a fresh authorization, with a fresh nonce, to buy another call.

post_payment_error.before_settlement: authorization released — the same header can be presented again
post_payment_error.after_settlement: settled at upstream acceptance: one automatic resubmission, then status `failed` with `refund_due` true
post_payment_error.note: No exit before settlement charges anything, and none of them keeps the single-use claim — an exit before the claim never took it, an exit after it hands it back — so the very same header can be presented again: a body that does not price, a payment the facilitator refuses, a facilitator that cannot be reached at all (503), an image URL that does not fetch as an image, an upstream queue that will not take the job, a brief that will not compile, a synthesis that returns no audio, a job row that cannot be written. After that point the answer depends on how the route delivers. The synchronous routes settle behind a response that already carries the product, so there is no window in which you have paid and have nothing. The asynchronous routes settle when the upstream ACCEPTS the render rather than when the file lands, so a render that fails afterwards has already been paid for: it is resubmitted once automatically on the same job row, and a second failure sets status `failed` with `refund_due` true.

refund.note: No automatic refund and no self-service one. There is no refund endpoint, no credit, no dispute endpoint and no reversal of a settled payment anywhere in this service. The mechanism is non-charge rather than refund: an authorization for work that was never accepted is never submitted, so no funds move at all. The single case where money moved and no product exists — an asynchronous render that failed twice — is reported as `refund_due` on the free GET /v1/jobs/{id} and refunded by hand against that job id, by mail to support@kino402.com. Anything else is that same address and a conversation, not a guaranteed remedy.

acceptance_observer.observed_from: {job_id, status_url} in the 200, then GET /v1/jobs/{id} until status is `completed` or `failed`
acceptance_observer.note: The buyer, from the 200 this service returns. No third party attests, no oracle is consulted and nothing has to be signed back: on the asynchronous routes the 200 carries {job_id, status_url} and the free, unauthenticated GET /v1/jobs/{id} is where you watch the render reach `completed` with its video_url or `failed` with its reason, and on the synchronous routes the 200 body IS the product — the compiled prompt as JSON, or the mp3. kino402 keeps its own settlement ledger, but that is an operator's record for reconciliation and it is not offered to the buyer as evidence.

silence_window.note: None. Nothing on this service becomes accepted by the passage of time: settlement is queued at delivery on the synchronous routes and at upstream acceptance on the asynchronous ones, and no timer anywhere converts a buyer's silence into acceptance, closes a complaint or finalises a charge that would otherwise be open. A job that failed after payment keeps reporting `refund_due` on every poll — that flag has no expiry, and not polling does not spend it.

Send one https photo and the product name; the clip opens and closes on that exact photo, with one slow move between — an orbit, a push-in, a float, a light sweep or a parallax drift — so it loops without a seam. You get back the compiled prompt with the job. Unpaid: 402 carrying the exact quote for this brief. Paid: the brief is compiled into a prompt, the render is submitted, and you get {job_id, compiled_prompt, status_url} back — poll the status url for the mp4 exactly as you would for /v1/generate. The compile runs only after payment verifies, and a compile that cannot produce a prompt is a 502 with nothing charged.

Paid: the brief is compiled and you get {prompt, render_plan, compiler} back in the response, synchronously, with no job to poll and no video produced. A single signed authorization buys exactly one call at the amount that call's own 402 quoted, and the whole quoted amount settles or nothing does — there is no partial, metered or per-second billing and no charge is ever split across a retry. kino402 prices are parametric, so the band published here is the floor and the ceiling this resource can quote; the unpaid 402 answering the body you actually sent is the authority on the number, and it is the number that settles.

hold.note: None. Verification is a read at the facilitator (verifyPayment in worker/kino.js), so nothing is reserved, escrowed or held: the signed authorization moves no funds until it is submitted at settle, which runs in ctx.waitUntil after the response has already been sent. An authorization that never reaches settle is simply never submitted, and no balance of yours was ever encumbered while it was outstanding.

idempotency.key: sha256(signed authorization: network + payer + nonce on EVM, network + transaction on Solana)
idempotency.note: There is no idempotency-key header. The key is the signed authorization itself, read out of the payment header — PAYMENT-SIGNATURE for x402 v2, X-PAYMENT for x402 v1, and PAYMENT-SIGNATURE is the one read when a request carries both: on Base the SHA-256 of the network, the payer address and the EIP-3009 nonce, on Solana of the network and the serialized transaction's decoded bytes (claimKeyOf in worker/kino.js). Re-encoding the same authorization — whitespace, key order, the other protocol version, a respelled base64 transaction — is therefore the same key, and a payment missing its network's authorization field is refused 402 `malformed_payment_header` before anything is claimed. The key is claimed single-use by claimPaymentOnce after the payment verifies and before any work is ordered. A second request carrying the same authorization, concurrently or an hour later, is answered 402 with invalidReason `payment_already_used` and the live terms re-offered: it submits no render, compiles no prompt, synthesises no audio and settles nothing. Sign a fresh authorization, with a fresh nonce, to buy another call.

post_payment_error.before_settlement: authorization released — the same header can be presented again
post_payment_error.after_settlement: none — settlement is queued only once the product is in the response
post_payment_error.note: No exit before settlement charges anything, and none of them keeps the single-use claim — an exit before the claim never took it, an exit after it hands it back — so the very same header can be presented again: a body that does not price, a payment the facilitator refuses, a facilitator that cannot be reached at all (503), an image URL that does not fetch as an image, an upstream queue that will not take the job, a brief that will not compile, a synthesis that returns no audio, a job row that cannot be written. After that point the answer depends on how the route delivers. The synchronous routes settle behind a response that already carries the product, so there is no window in which you have paid and have nothing. The asynchronous routes settle when the upstream ACCEPTS the render rather than when the file lands, so a render that fails afterwards has already been paid for: it is resubmitted once automatically on the same job row, and a second failure sets status `failed` with `refund_due` true.

refund.note: No automatic refund and no self-service one. There is no refund endpoint, no credit, no dispute endpoint and no reversal of a settled payment anywhere in this service. The mechanism is non-charge rather than refund: an authorization for work that was never accepted is never submitted, so no funds move at all. The single case where money moved and no product exists — an asynchronous render that failed twice — is reported as `refund_due` on the free GET /v1/jobs/{id} and refunded by hand against that job id, by mail to support@kino402.com. Anything else is that same address and a conversation, not a guaranteed remedy.

acceptance_observer.observed_from: the 200 response body, which is the product
acceptance_observer.note: The buyer, from the 200 this service returns. No third party attests, no oracle is consulted and nothing has to be signed back: on the asynchronous routes the 200 carries {job_id, status_url} and the free, unauthenticated GET /v1/jobs/{id} is where you watch the render reach `completed` with its video_url or `failed` with its reason, and on the synchronous routes the 200 body IS the product — the compiled prompt as JSON, or the mp3. kino402 keeps its own settlement ledger, but that is an operator's record for reconciliation and it is not offered to the buyer as evidence.

silence_window.note: None. Nothing on this service becomes accepted by the passage of time: settlement is queued at delivery on the synchronous routes and at upstream acceptance on the asynchronous ones, and no timer anywhere converts a buyer's silence into acceptance, closes a complaint or finalises a charge that would otherwise be open. A job that failed after payment keeps reporting `refund_due` on every poll — that flag has no expiry, and not polling does not spend it.
